newsitem.title: USA: Pamela Harriman's estate goes on sale. [CORRECTED 22:43 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Pamela Harriman's estate goes on sale. [CORRECTED 22:43 GMT]

text.p: The possessions of Pamela Harriman, one of the century's best-connected women, go on sale on Monday night after a weekend in which New Yorkers tested her sofas, sized up her china and admired her mementos of the rich and famous.

The sale items include everything from a photograph of her at the Yalta Conference with Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill to a painting of a staircase in Capri by a 22-year-old John Singer Sargent estimated to be worth about $1 million.

From Monday night through Wednesday afternoon, Sotheby's will auction off more than 1,150 items from the former U.S. ambassador to France's estate less than four months after her death at age 76 after suffering a stroke while swimming at a Paris hotel.

Sotheby's estimates the three-day sale could fetch from about $3 million to almost $6 million, although the prices could go higher if the public decides to accord the auction the same sort of "garage sale" celebrity status it has previously bestowed on the estate sales of the Duchess of Windsor and Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis.

Although the auction house was packed over the weekend with people trying out Harriman's chairs and ogling her antique French and English furniture, the sale so far has not generated the feeding frenzy that accompanied last year's sale of Onassis's belongings.
The Onassis sale realised more than $135 million for her heirs as the public bid frantically for everything from her fake pearls to her used pillows.

Pamela Harriman, a member of a minor English noble family, was Winston Churchill's daughter-in-law for the brief wartime period in which she was married to his son Randolph. She established a life-long friendship with Sir Winston and even accompanied him to Yalta as an aide.

She went on to marry Broadway and Hollywood producer Leland Hayward (corrects from Haywood) and millionaire Democratic Party activist W. Averell Harriman. In between were affairs with some of the century's most prominent men, including Aly Khan, Fiat owner Gianni Agnelli and Greek shipping magnate Stavros (corrects from Starvos) Niarchos.
Sotheby's vice president C. Hugh Hildesley said that while there were similarities with the Onassis sale, the two women clearly were different and do not occupy the same status in the public mind.
"There is a wonderful selection of Churchill items, including the Yalta photographs and paintings by Churchill as well. You could set up an apartment with the furniture and china on sale," he said.

Among the items on sale is the pen that President John F. Kennedy used to sign the Nuclear Test Ban Treaty with Russia. The desk Kennedy sat at to sign the treaty was auctioned off at the Onassis sale.
